extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in CS371 Cognitive Science and readers interested in cognitive theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain historical and contemporary theories of humor, with emphasis on the Hurley/Dennett/Adams evolutionary model and its cognitive/phenomenological implications. Suitable as lecture notes or a concise overview for students learning theories of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: "that the passion of laughter is nothing else but sudden glory arising from some sudden conception of some eminency in ourselves, by comparison with the infirmity of others..." (Thomas Hobbes). Superiority theories hold that feelings of superiority over others give rise to humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains phenomena like schadenfreude; traces to Aristotle/Plato and popularized by Hobbes. Related reverse formulation (Inferiority Theory by Robert Solomon) accounts for self-deprecating humor. Limitation: does not account for many forms of humor (e.g., non-sequitur, absurdist comedy such as Monty Python).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor derives from misplaced expectations or perceived incongruity — a sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing (Kant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically rooted (Aristotle: 'gives a twist'), refined by Kant and Schopenhauer. Useful for explaining a wide range of jokes but criticized as too broad; may conflate the object that causes humor with the observer's response, so lacks specificity in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurley Model — humor as evolutionary incentive for mental debugging
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved as a mechanism to incentivize a costly cognitive 'garbage collection' or debugging process: the perception of humor bribes the brain to resolve mistaken assumptions and maintain data integrity in mental representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to other evolved incentives (pain avoidance, sexual attraction, cuteness, sweetness). Argues the brain continuously makes approximations and assumptions; humor rewards the expensive process of detecting and correcting those errors. Use this model to connect cognitive error-detection with affective reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dennett formalization of proto-humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Proto- or first-person humor occurs when an active element covertly enters a mental space, is taken to be true (epistemically committed) within that space, is diagnosed to be false in that space (loses in an epistemic reconciliation), and the discovery is not accompanied by strong negative emotional valence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal clause identifies the cognitive structure that produces amusement: covert acceptance + reconciliation leading to non-threatening discovery. Good for analyzing when and why a mental bug yields amusement rather than alarm or shame. Emphasizes epistemic commitment and the absence of strong negative emotion as key conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super-normal stimuli in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians (and cultural evolution) can craft exaggerated stimuli that elicit stronger humor responses than naturalistic inputs, analogous to Tinbergen's super-normal stimuli (e.g., gull chicks pecking a painted needle more than a real beak).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tinbergen's gull experiments; junk food as exaggerated stimuli for cravings. Implication: jokes can be intentionally designed ('intelligent design' by comedians) to amplify cognitive triggers of the humor response. Use this concept to analyze joke construction and why certain exaggerations feel funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenology of humor (contextuality and dependency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is not an intrinsic property of stimuli but a second-order quality dependent on the observer's disposition, mental state, and assumptions (Lockean second-order quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains cultural specificity of jokes and why making key facts explicit can ruin a joke (example: 'A man walks into a bar (beat) ouch.' — explicating the assumed meaning removes the effect). Highlights importance of shared assumptions, timing, and implicitness for successful humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional Stance and social forms of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the intentional stance (interpreting others as having minds and intentions) allows appreciation of mental bugs in others, producing social forms of humor such as superiority, ingroup/outgroup effects, and jokes about others' mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects the proto-humor account (self-recognized mental bugs) to social humor: once we interpret others as agents, their cognitive errors become sources of amusement. Use to analyze social dynamics of laughter and how perspective-taking influences what audiences find funny.
